title: From five browser mini-games to a 5-episode cartoon and back to a playable game
author: gameover_com
selftext:
Hi! We make HTML mini-games with AI. For us, the best part of a game is its characters and the world you want to spend time in, and we think that's also what brings players back. So we wanted a way to meet a game's characters before pressing play, with a story that keeps growing between releases. We describe here our Claude Code pipeline for creating GO TV and our first featured game. Snail Express: Eventually follows a very slow snail courier delivering one parcel into the world of another game from our catalog.

The original games: The five featured games are single HTML files of 33–115 KB. Snail Express 3D and Baby Dragon use three.js; Blimp Postie and Bobba Tea Madness are plain Canvas 2D. Because everything lives in one file, the model can read a whole game in one pass, which the next steps depend on.

The episodes: We built Season 1 step by step with Opus 5.5 running on Claude Code on medium effort, with human review and guidance between steps. Afterwards we folded the steps into one master prompt plus a shared kit and build script, so a new series can start from a single request:

\- World bible: Opus 5.5 reads a game's code and returns JSON with its palette, characters, worlds, control verbs and exact HUD and tutorial strings, directing it to "never invent canon".

\- Show runner: five episodes from those bibles. Every punchline has to depend on the host game's core mechanic.

\- Art bible, then second-accurate beat sheets with camera, speech bubbles and timed sound cues.

\- Animation: each episode is one procedural Canvas file of about 71 KB, with no image or audio files. More than 80% of each file is lines shared by all five episodes (character rigs, bubbles, title and end cards, a Web Audio music bed).

\- Export: a Playwright script steps the episode clock at 30 fps and renders the audio offline on the same clock, then ffmpeg writes a 1920×1080 mp4. The YouTube Shorts version places that video inside a vertical 1080×1920 frame.

The playable season: One 104 KB HTML file with five chapters, one per episode: a delivery window, a sky road, an egg that hatches mid-level, a pearl toss and an overhead mower race. 75 of its 112 functions are byte-identical to episode 1's, so the game and the show share the same cast. We playtested and tuned the feel with arithmetic instead of adjectives. For example, the first jump (185 px peak) couldn't clear a rock, so we set a rule: the ground covered in the air must be wider than the hitbox plus the widest obstacle. That gave a combination of peak and air time such that every ground obstacle is clearable at the slowest speed.

Every end card links to its featured game. On YouTube, about 80% of views came from the vertical Shorts cut.

If you've made video from your own game code, how did you keep characters consistent between the video and the game? Sharing draw functions worked for us, tying the art style to what Canvas code can draw for 2D games.

Thanks for reading!
